editorial.hook: Two peasants chase war profits and glory; the ghosts are the least frightening thing.
editorial.synopsis: Sixteenth-century Japan, civil war burning across the countryside. A potter sees that soldiers will pay anything for his wares and his brother-in-law sees a chance to become a samurai, and both leave their wives behind to chase what they want. The potter is taken in by a noblewoman in a mansion that seems to float in mist; the other man buys armour with stolen money. Mizoguchi films it in long gliding takes — a boat crossing a lake in fog is one of the most beautiful shots ever made — and lets the ghost story and the war story become the same story about men who cannot see what they have. The return home, at the end, is a single unbroken camera movement around a room, and it will undo you.
editorial.whyItMatters: Silver Lion at Venice in 1953 and 58th on TSPDT's list; the film that introduced Mizoguchi to the West alongside Rashomon, and the summit of his flowing long take — a camera that moves like water and makes the supernatural feel like grief.

title: A Matter of Life and Death

editorial.hook: A pilot who should have died falls in love instead, and heaven sends a lawyer.
editorial.synopsis: A British bomber pilot with a burning plane and no parachute spends his last minutes on the radio with an American operator, and jumps. He wakes up on a beach, alive — a clerical error in the afterlife, which is running behind because of the war. By the time the heavenly messenger finds him he has met the radio operator and fallen in love, and he demands a trial for the right to stay. Powell and Pressburger shot earth in Technicolor and heaven in pearly black and white, built a stairway that climbs through the stars, and staged the trial as a debate between Britain and America that is also about whether love outranks the rules. It is witty, humane, and formally dazzling, and it was made to comfort a nation at the end of a war.
editorial.whyItMatters: Seventy-eighth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and Powell and Pressburger's most beloved film; the inversion of colour and monochrome, the operating-theatre sequence and the escalator to heaven are landmarks of what British cinema could imagine.

editorial.hook: Varda with a small digital camera, filming people who pick up what others leave behind.
editorial.synopsis: Agnès Varda, in her seventies, buys a small digital camera and sets off across France to meet gleaners — people who gather what is left after the harvest: potatoes rejected for being the wrong shape, grapes left on the vine, food from bins behind supermarkets, furniture from pavements. She films a lawyer standing in a cabbage field quoting the law on gleaning, a man who has lived on discarded food for ten years and teaches literacy at night, artists who build with junk. And she films her own hand, her own greying hair, lets the lens cap dance when she forgets to turn the camera off. It is a film about waste and about looking, and it is one of the most generous films ever made.
editorial.whyItMatters: Sixty-seventh in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll — the highest-placed film of the century's first decade — and the work that opened the digital essay film; Varda showed that a cheap camera in the right hands was not a compromise but a liberation.

editorial.hook: A writer, his family, and a hotel closed for the winter that has its own ideas.
editorial.synopsis: A would-be writer takes a job as winter caretaker of a vast, empty hotel in the Colorado mountains, and brings his wife and his small son, who has a gift he doesn't have a word for. The snow closes the roads. The hotel's corridors, filmed with a Steadicam that glides a few inches behind the boy's tricycle, are too wide and too symmetrical and go on too long. Kubrick took Stephen King's ghost story and drained the explanations from it, so that what remains is a family coming apart in a building that encourages them, and images — a lift of blood, twin girls, a typewriter — that have passed into the culture whether you have seen the film or not. It is cold and funny and it does not resolve.
editorial.whyItMatters: Eighty-eighth in the 2022 critics' poll after decades of being treated as Kubrick's mistake; the film that made the horror genre a legitimate field for formal ambition, and whose ambiguities have sustained an entire documentary of interpretations.

editorial.hook: Two women in Paris, a sweet that lets them enter a house where the same day repeats.
editorial.synopsis: A librarian in a Paris park sees a woman drop her sunglasses and scarf, Alice-fashion, and follows. The two become friends, then roommates, then conspirators, and one of them starts coming home dazed from a house in a quiet street with a sweet in her mouth. The sweet, they discover, is the key: eat it and you remember an afternoon inside the house, where a melodrama about a widower, two women and a sick child plays out the same way every day. So they go in together, and then they go in to change it. Rivette lets the film run over three hours and improvise its way forward, and the result is the closest cinema has come to the feeling of two friends inventing a game that becomes a world.
editorial.whyItMatters: Seventy-eighth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the French New Wave's great late experiment; its nested fictions and female friendship are the direct source of Desperately Seeking Susan, of Mulholland Drive's structure and of the idea that a film can be a playground.

editorial.hook: A London photographer enlarges a shot from a park until he sees a body — or doesn't.
editorial.synopsis: A fashion photographer in swinging London, bored by models and his own success, wanders into a park and photographs a couple embracing. The woman follows him and wants the film back, badly. He develops it, enlarges it, enlarges it again, pinning the prints across his studio wall, and in the grain of the leaves there seems to be a hand with a gun, and later, a body. Antonioni shot London in colours he had the grass painted to achieve, with the Yardbirds in a club and mimes playing tennis without a ball, and the mystery dissolves the closer you look — which is the subject. By the end you are no longer sure what the photographer saw, or whether seeing is what photographs do.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1967 and Antonioni's international breakthrough; the film that turned a thriller premise into an essay on the unreliability of the image, remade in spirit by Coppola as The Conversation and De Palma as Blow Out.

editorial.hook: A boy has his classmate's notebook by mistake and crosses two villages to return it.
editorial.synopsis: A schoolteacher in a village in northern Iran threatens to expel a boy who keeps forgetting his homework notebook. That afternoon his classmate realises he has taken the boy's notebook home by mistake. If he doesn't return it, his friend will be expelled. So he sets off, against his mother's orders, to the next village, where he does not know the house, up and down a zigzag path on a bare hill, asking everyone, getting sent wrong, meeting an old carpenter who talks too slowly. That is the whole plot. Kiarostami films it with the patience of the boy himself, and the moral stakes — a child's sense that a promise is absolute — become as tense as anything in a thriller.
editorial.whyItMatters: The first of Kiarostami's Koker trilogy and 157th in the 2022 critics' poll; the film that showed the world Iranian cinema's method — children, real villages, an ethical question pursued without a plot — and founded the lineage that runs through Panahi and Majidi.

editorial.hook: A pair of earrings sold, bought back, given away and returned, until they ruin everyone.
editorial.synopsis: A countess in belle-époque Paris quietly sells the diamond earrings her husband gave her to cover her debts, and tells him they were lost. The jeweller sells them back to the husband; he gives them to his mistress, who gambles them away in Constantinople; an Italian diplomat buys them, comes to Paris, and falls in love with the countess. He gives her the earrings. Ophüls films this circle in a camera that never stops moving — through ballrooms, up staircases, around dancers in a waltz that compresses weeks into one shot — and what begins as a frivolous comedy of a society woman's vanity turns, so gradually you don't see it happen, into tragedy. Danielle Darrieux's face in the last reel is the whole history of a heart learning it is serious.
editorial.whyItMatters: Ninetieth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the film Stanley Kubrick and Paul Thomas Anderson have both named as perfect; Ophüls' moving camera is the ancestor of the Steadicam long take and of every film in which style is the content.

editorial.hook: A young man in Paris takes up theft as a vocation, filmed as hands and glances.
editorial.synopsis: A young man in a Paris attic room decides to become a pickpocket — not for money, exactly, but because he believes certain men are above the law and wants to find out if he is one. He learns the craft from a professional, and Bresson films the lessons and the thefts at racetracks and on the Métro as ballets of hands: wallets lifted from inside jackets, a watch slipped off a wrist, a newspaper used as a screen. The young man's face shows almost nothing; the voice-over tells you what he will not. A police inspector circles him like a friend. A neighbour's daughter waits. It is seventy-five minutes long and ends with one of the great lines in cinema, spoken through prison bars.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' top ten in 1959 and the film Paul Schrader rewrote as Taxi Driver and American Gigolo; Bresson's adaptation of Crime and Punishment to the gestures of theft is the purest demonstration that cinema can show a soul through the movements of a hand.

editorial.hook: A woman steals money and stops at a motel. Nothing after that is what it seems.
editorial.synopsis: A secretary in Phoenix steals forty thousand dollars from her employer to marry her lover and drives north, paranoid, through rain, and pulls in at a motel off the old highway run by a shy young man who lives with his mother in the house up the hill. Hitchcock shot it quickly, in black and white, with his television crew, to prove he could make something cheap and shocking, and it is the most carefully constructed film of his career: a first act that lies about what kind of film this is, a shower sequence of seventy-eight shots in forty-five seconds, Bernard Herrmann's screaming violins. Audiences were not admitted after the start. It changed what could be shown, and what could be done to an audience's trust.
editorial.whyItMatters: Thirty-first in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the film that invented the modern horror film and the modern twist; Hitchcock's cruellest trick on his audience, and the clearest demonstration that editing can do violence more effectively than showing it.

editorial.hook: Two lovesick Hong Kong cops, a woman in a blonde wig, and one song on repeat.
editorial.synopsis: Two stories of two Hong Kong policemen, barely connected. In the first, a cop whose girlfriend has left him buys a tin of pineapple with a May 1st expiry date every night for a month, and brushes against a woman in a blonde wig and sunglasses who is running drugs. In the second, another cop eats at the same snack bar every night, and the new girl behind the counter falls for him and starts breaking into his flat while he's out to rearrange his life. Wong shot it in weeks between other projects, hand-held, in smeared slow motion, with 'California Dreamin'' playing until it becomes a character, and it has the energy of a city that never sleeps and never says what it means.
editorial.whyItMatters: Eighty-eighth in the 2022 critics' poll and the film that made Wong Kar-wai an international name — Tarantino distributed it in America; its step-printed motion and jukebox soundtrack became the look of the 1990s, and the second story is one of cinema's great accounts of being quietly in love.

editorial.hook: A bomb in a car trunk on the border, a corrupt cop, and a three-minute opening shot.
editorial.synopsis: A bomb is placed in the trunk of a car in a Mexican border town, and the camera follows it — over rooftops, through streets, past a Mexican narcotics officer and his American bride walking to the crossing — for three and a half unbroken minutes until it goes off. The American cop who arrives to investigate is a bloated monument of corruption played by Welles himself, planting evidence because he knows who's guilty. Welles shot it in Venice, California, dressed as Tijuana, in deep shadows and canted angles, with Marlene Dietrich in a black wig telling fortunes. The studio recut it; his fifty-eight-page memo on how it should be assembled was finally followed in 1998. It is the last film noir and the strangest.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' film of the year in 1958 — the French saw what Hollywood threw away — and 42nd on TSPDT's list; the opening shot is the most studied long take in cinema, and the film's portrait of a lawman gone rotten is the dark mirror of every police procedural since.

editorial.hook: Four brothels in 1880s Shanghai, lit by oil lamps, in thirty-eight shots and no exteriors.
editorial.synopsis: Shanghai's flower houses in the 1880s — elegant brothels where wealthy men spend their evenings drinking, gambling and conducting long, delicate negotiations with the courtesans who run them. A man is drifting from one woman to another and she knows it; a courtesan wants to buy her freedom; another is in debt; a girl is being groomed to replace someone. Hou films the entire thing indoors, by lamplight, in long slow takes that drift across tables and fade to black, and never leaves the rooms — the outside world exists only as what the characters say about it. Nothing is dramatised. Everything is implied, in a glance over an opium pipe or a sum of money mentioned at dinner.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' film of the year in 1998 and the most radical formal object in Hou's career; thirty-eight shots, one per scene, each a slow drift of lamplight across faces — a film that asks you to watch the way you would listen, and which Scorsese has called one of the most beautiful ever made.

editorial.hook: King Lear in feudal Japan: an old warlord divides his kingdom and burns down the world.
editorial.synopsis: An old warlord divides his domain between his three sons, banishes the one who tells him the truth, and finds within weeks that the other two have no further use for him. Kurosawa, seventy-five and nearly blind, spent a decade painting the storyboards and then built the castles to burn them down. The siege at the film's centre is staged without sound — only Tōru Takemitsu's score — as arrows pour into a fortress and the old man walks out through the flames with his mind gone. The colours of the armies, red, yellow and blue, turn the battlefields into a moving painting of a world dissolving. There is a jester, a vengeful daughter-in-law and a blind boy with a flute on a cliff at dusk.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' top ten in 1985 and Kurosawa's last epic; Lear transposed to the Sengoku period with a grief about history that is entirely his own, and the most expensive Japanese film ever made at the time — a final statement about chaos from the director who had spent a career ordering it.

editorial.hook: Seven hours in a collapsing Hungarian farm, in rain, mud and long black-and-white takes.
editorial.synopsis: A collective farm on the Hungarian plain in the last days of communism, in autumn rain that never stops. The farmers have the year's money and plan to run off with it; a man they thought was dead is seen walking back along the road; a little girl poisons her cat and then herself; a doctor sits at his window drinking and writing down everything his neighbours do. Tarr tells it in twelve chapters that move forward and back like the steps of a tango, in takes that run eight or ten minutes — cows leaving a barn, two men walking into wind, a drunken dance in a bar that goes on and on. It is seven hours and twelve minutes and the time is the subject. You come out of it changed, if only by the weather.
editorial.whyItMatters: Seventy-eighth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the summit of slow cinema; Tarr's long takes and Mihály Víg's accordion score defined a way of filming time that Gus Van Sant, Lav Diaz and a generation of festival directors have followed, and Susan Sontag said she'd watch it every year of her life.

editorial.hook: A film crew waits in a Kurdish village for an old woman to die. She keeps not dying.
editorial.synopsis: A man from Tehran arrives in a remote Kurdish village with a crew we never see, for reasons he won't give — he is waiting, it becomes clear, for a very old woman to die so he can film the mourning rituals. She rallies. He waits. His phone only works on the hilltop by the cemetery, so he drives up there a dozen times, and talks to a man digging a hole whose face we also never see. He gets a shave. He talks to a boy. He recites a poem by Forugh Farrokhzad to a girl milking a cow in the dark. Kiarostami leaves more than a dozen characters off screen entirely and makes a film about a man who is in a place and not present in it — until, slowly, he is.
editorial.whyItMatters: Grand Jury Prize at Venice 1999 and Cahiers' second-best of the year; Kiarostami's most elusive film, which keeps its subject out of frame and finds its meaning in a bone, a turtle and a poem — the model for a cinema of absence that Apichatpong and Reichardt have both acknowledged.

editorial.hook: A paleontologist, an heiress, a leopard named Baby, and a dog with a dinosaur bone.
editorial.synopsis: A mild paleontologist one day from completing his brontosaurus and marrying his assistant meets an heiress on a golf course who takes his ball, his car and then his life. She has a tame leopard called Baby that responds to 'I Can't Give You Anything but Love'; her dog buries the dinosaur's last bone; a second leopard, not tame, gets loose in Connecticut. Hawks runs it faster than any comedy before it, with Katharine Hepburn and Cary Grant talking over each other for ninety minutes while the plot falls apart around them, and the chaos is the courtship. It lost money, Hepburn was declared box-office poison, and it is the most purely joyful film Hollywood ever made.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 124 on TSPDT's list and the definitive screwball comedy; the Cahiers critics' admiration for Hawks began with films like this, and its structure — a controlled man undone by an anarchic woman — has been the template for romantic comedy ever since.

editorial.hook: Twenty-four characters, five days in Nashville, and a political rally at the end.
editorial.synopsis: Five days in Nashville around a country music festival and a presidential campaign nobody has met the candidate of: a star having a breakdown, a would-be singer who can't sing, a BBC reporter who understands nothing, a soldier guarding a woman he loves from afar, a gospel singer with deaf children, a drifter with a violin case. Twenty-four of them. Altman lets them overlap — his eight-track sound records everyone at once, and you choose who to listen to — and the songs, written and sung by the actors, are the film's real dialogue. It is funny, sprawling and ominous, and the final concert at the Parthenon replica, with a flag and a shot, is one of the great endings about a country.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 90 on TSPDT's list and the peak of Altman's ensemble method; the film that proved a narrative could be a mosaic — Paul Thomas Anderson's Magnolia and every multi-strand drama since descend from it — and the most prescient American film about celebrity and politics.

editorial.hook: A woman loses her husband and child in a crash and tries to want nothing at all.
editorial.synopsis: A woman survives the car crash that kills her composer husband and their small daughter, and decides to disappear: sells the house, moves to a Paris flat where no one knows her, drops the manuscript of her husband's unfinished symphony in a rubbish truck, swims laps alone in a blue pool. Kieślowski films her refusal in blue — a chandelier of blue glass, a sugar cube soaking up coffee in close-up, the screen fading to black when the music in her head starts and she can't stop it. Juliette Binoche barely speaks. The world keeps arriving anyway: a neighbour, a mouse, a stripper downstairs, a woman carrying her husband's child. Liberty, the first colour of the French flag, turns out to be the hardest.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Lion at Venice in 1993 and the first panel of Kieślowski's final trilogy; a film about grief as a kind of freedom, carried by Binoche's stillness and Zbigniew Preisner's score, and the clearest statement of Kieślowski's belief that the metaphysical lives in sugar cubes and traffic.

editorial.hook: A boy in Miami learns who he is in three chapters, three actors, and one moonlit beach.
editorial.synopsis: A small, silent boy in Liberty City, Miami, with a mother losing herself to crack, is found hiding in an abandoned flat by a drug dealer who takes him home, feeds him, and teaches him to swim in the ocean — holding his head above the water. The film follows him in three chapters, with three actors, through a childhood, an adolescence and a hard-shelled manhood that has buried the boy entirely, and through one night on a beach with his only friend that neither of them can forget. Jenkins films Miami in saturated blues and purples and lets the camera stay on faces for a long time without speaking. The last half hour is two men at a diner table, and it is as tense and tender as anything in cinema.
editorial.whyItMatters: Sixtieth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the Best Picture winner that changed what the Academy's choice could look like; a film about Black queer masculinity made in the language of Wong Kar-wai and Claire Denis, and the work that made Jenkins the most important American director of his generation.

editorial.hook: A husband dead in the snow, a wife on trial, and a blind son who heard something.
editorial.synopsis: A German novelist lives in a chalet in the French Alps with her French husband, also a writer, and their eleven-year-old son, who is partly blind. The son comes back from a walk with his dog and finds his father dead in the snow below the attic window. There is no witness. The wife is charged, and the film becomes her trial — a dissection of a marriage conducted by lawyers who never met it, with a recording of one argument played to the court and acted out in flashback, and a son who has to decide what he believes about his mother in order to go on living with her. Triet never tells you what happened. Sandra Hüller's performance is the film's argument that no one could.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 2023 and Cahiers' third-best of the year; a courtroom drama that uses the genre to ask whether a marriage can be known from outside, and the film that made Hüller and the Border Collie Messi the faces of the year's cinema.

editorial.hook: A sheriff, a drunk, an old man and a kid hold a jail against a rancher's army, slowly.
editorial.synopsis: A sheriff in a Texas border town arrests a rancher's brother for murder and has to hold him in the jail until the marshal arrives in a week, with the rancher's gunmen filling the town. His deputies are a drunk trying to dry out, a limping old man with a shotgun, and, eventually, a young gunslinger who sings. Hawks made it as an answer to High Noon — where Gary Cooper begged the town for help, this sheriff refuses it — and the film is less about the siege than about the week: men in a room, learning each other, a woman who stays at the hotel and won't be told to leave. Dean Martin and Ricky Nelson sing a song together with Walter Brennan on harmonica, and nothing in the Western is more relaxed or more sure.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' top ten in 1959 and 63rd on TSPDT's list; the film the French critics held up as proof of Hawks' authorship — professionalism, friendship and competence as a moral code — and the Western Tarantino says he shows to anyone he's considering being friends with.

editorial.hook: A childhood in a theatre family, a Christmas, a death, and a stepfather like winter.
editorial.synopsis: Uppsala, 1907. A large, warm, theatrical family — grandmother, uncles, actors, servants, a lantern-lit Christmas Eve that fills the first hour — seen through the eyes of a boy who has a magic lantern and a tendency to see ghosts. Then his father dies on stage rehearsing Hamlet, and his mother marries a bishop, and the children are moved from a house full of red velvet and candlelight to a whitewashed one full of rules and bare floors. Bergman made it as his farewell to cinema, and it has everything he knew: the cruelty of faith, the consolation of theatre, a grandmother who understands, a Jewish antiques dealer whose shop contains a breathing mummy and a way out. It is his most generous film by far.
editorial.whyItMatters: Fifty-second in the 2022 Sight & Sound directors' poll and the five-hour television version is the definitive one; four Academy Awards and Bergman's own account of how he became an artist — a child's revenge on a cold father, made with love.

editorial.hook: A year on a Lombard farm in the 1890s, played by the farmers themselves.
editorial.synopsis: Four tenant families share a farmhouse on an estate in Lombardy in the 1890s, and the film is their year: slaughtering a pig, a wedding, a courtship conducted walking home from church, a grandfather growing tomatoes in secret so they'll ripen early, a baby, a landlord who takes two-thirds of everything. One family's boy is clever and the priest says he should go to school, six kilometres away. He wears through his clogs, and his father cuts down a tree on the landlord's land to make him new ones. Olmi shot it in Bergamasque dialect with real farmers from the villages around, in natural light, over three hours, and it is as patient and exact as a season.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1978 and the last great flowering of Neorealism's method — non-actors, real places, no plot but life; Olmi's film is the bridge from De Sica to the Dardennes and Alice Rohrwacher, who made Happy as Lazzaro in direct homage to it.

editorial.hook: A Moscow girl loses her fiancé to the war, and the camera runs, spins and climbs with her.
editorial.synopsis: Moscow, June 1941. A young woman and her fiancé watch cranes fly over the river at dawn; the next day Germany invades and he volunteers. She misses his departure in the crowd — the camera plunges into the crush and spins with her — and then the letters stop, and his cousin, a pianist who stayed behind, forces himself on her during an air raid. She marries him out of shame. Kalatozov and his cameraman Sergei Urusevsky shot it with a wildness Soviet cinema had never allowed: handheld runs up stairwells, a dying soldier's spinning view of birch trees, a wide-angle lens that makes faces loom. It was the first Soviet film to admit that the war was lived by people and not only by the people.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1958 — the only Soviet film ever to win it — and the breakthrough of the post-Stalin thaw; Urusevsky's camera is the direct ancestor of the Steadicam long take, and the film's grief without heroics made it the model for every war film that followed in the East.

editorial.hook: A surveillance expert records a couple in a park, and the tape starts saying more.
editorial.synopsis: The best wiretapper on the West Coast records a young couple walking in circles through Union Square in San Francisco for a corporate client, from three microphones, and spends the film reconstructing the conversation — filtering, synchronising, replaying — until one sentence comes clear and seems to mean that someone is going to be killed. He is a Catholic who believes he is not responsible for what he records. Coppola made it between the two Godfathers, and it is the quieter and in some ways the more frightening film: Gene Hackman in a translucent raincoat, a saxophone played alone in an empty flat, and a sound design by Walter Murch in which the tape's meaning changes as the hearing does.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1974 and the New Hollywood film most precisely about its own time — released weeks before Nixon resigned — and about ours; the ancestor of every paranoid thriller since, and the clearest demonstration that sound can be a film's subject rather than its accompaniment.

editorial.hook: Two friends and the woman they both love, across twenty years and one war.
editorial.synopsis: Paris before the Great War. An Austrian and a Frenchman are inseparable — they box, translate, chase girls, see a statue with a smile that undoes them both — and then they meet the woman who has the statue's smile, and she marries one and loves the other and belongs to neither. The war separates the friends across the trenches; after it, the three try to live together in a chalet on the Rhine and in a house outside Paris. Truffaut narrates in a rush, freeze-frames Jeanne Moreau mid-laugh, uses newsreel footage and a bicycle race and a song she sings about a whirlwind, and the film's exhilaration is all the more wrenching for what you know is coming. It is the most joyful tragedy in cinema.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' second-best film of 1962 and 98th on TSPDT's list; the New Wave's most beloved film, whose speed and lightness — narration, freeze frames, a camera that can't sit still — fed directly into Scorsese and every film that has tried to make a love triangle feel like freedom.

editorial.hook: Paris's theatre street in the 1830s, a mime in love, made in secret under occupation.
editorial.synopsis: The Boulevard du Temple in Paris in the 1830s, called the Boulevard of Crime for its melodramas, and the four men who love the same woman: a mime of genius who cannot speak his love, an actor who can speak nothing else, a murderer-poet, and a count who buys her. Carné and the poet Jacques Prévert made it during the Occupation with a crew hiding Resistance members and Jews, built the whole boulevard on a lot in Nice, and filled it with eighteen hundred extras. It is three hours of theatre about theatre — the 'paradise' is the cheap seats in the gods — and the mime Baptiste, played by Jean-Louis Barrault, is one of the great performances of silence in a sound film. The last shot, a man lost in a carnival crowd, is unbearable.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 74 on TSPDT's list and the film French critics have called their Gone with the Wind — made in defiance of the Nazis and released as Paris was liberated; the summit of poetic realism and the French cinema the New Wave both rebelled against and could not stop loving.

editorial.hook: A carpenter with a perfect family takes a mistress and sees no reason it can't be happy.
editorial.synopsis: A young carpenter in a Paris suburb has a wife he adores, two small children, and Sunday picnics in sun-dappled woods to Mozart. He meets a woman at the post office and starts an affair and sees no contradiction: he loves them both, he tells his wife, and there is more happiness now, not less. Varda shoots it in the colours of an Impressionist painting and a washing-powder advert — sunflowers, yellow dresses, a lake in summer — and lets the horror of his reasoning arrive without ever raising the film's voice. What happens next, and how quickly life rearranges itself around it, is one of the coldest things she ever filmed, and the warm colours never change.
editorial.whyItMatters: Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize at Berlin in 1965 and the most quietly savage film of the New Wave; Varda's critique of the happy family, made in the visual language of its own advertising, and a film whose ending has been argued about for sixty years.

editorial.hook: One Taiwanese family from the end of Japanese rule to the massacre of 1947.
editorial.synopsis: Taiwan, 1945 to 1949, and one family of four brothers: a restaurant owner, a man lost in the war, a smuggler who comes back from Shanghai broken, and a deaf-mute photographer who falls in love with a nurse and communicates with her in handwritten notes that appear on screen as intertitles. The Japanese leave; the Nationalists arrive from the mainland; and in February 1947 the new government opens fire on protesters and begins a slaughter the island was forbidden to speak of for forty years. Hou films all of it from the middle distance, in long still takes through doorways, dinner tables and hospital corridors, so that history is what happens at the edge of the frame while people eat.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Lion 1989 — the first for a Taiwanese film — and the first film to depict the 28 February massacre, made the year martial law ended; the summit of New Taiwanese Cinema's method of showing history through a family's rooms, and Hou's masterwork.

editorial.hook: Mail pilots in a fog-bound Andean port, flying a pass that kills them one by one.
editorial.synopsis: A ramshackle air-mail outfit in a port at the foot of the Andes flies the mail over a pass that is fogged in half the year, and the men who fly it have a code: don't talk about the ones who don't come back. A showgirl stranded between boats falls for the boss, who has rules about women too; a pilot everyone despises arrives with a wife who turns out to be the boss's old flame. Hawks shot it mostly on a studio set with a model mountain and a lot of fog, and it is one of the great films about work — about men doing something dangerous well, and the ritual that lets them keep doing it. 'Who's Joe?' is the line, and it is as hard as anything in Hemingway.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 122 in the 2022 critics' poll and the purest statement of Hawks' ethic — professionalism as grace under pressure — that the Cahiers critics built auteur theory on; Jean Arthur and Cary Grant, Rita Hayworth's breakthrough, and a template for the ensemble adventure film.

editorial.hook: Hulot's nephew prefers his uncle's crumbling quarter to his parents' automated house.
editorial.synopsis: A small boy lives with his parents in an ultra-modern house in a new Paris suburb — a fish fountain that is switched on only for guests, a kitchen that beeps, a garden of stepping stones that must be walked on correctly. His uncle, Monsieur Hulot, lives across the vacant lot in an old quarter where the stairs go in every direction and a dog chases a cart every morning. The boy prefers the uncle. The father gets Hulot a job at his plastic-hose factory. Tati films the modern house as a machine for making people ridiculous — the circular windows that become eyes at night are the film's most famous image — and the old quarter as a place where accidents are still allowed. The gags are quiet and exact and the sound is its own comedy.
editorial.whyItMatters: Jury Prize at Cannes 1958 and the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film; Tati's gentlest satire of modernity and the step toward PlayTime, in which the house itself became the whole film — a comedy of design that architects still screen.

editorial.hook: An editor tries to stop his star reporter — and ex-wife — from quitting, at full speed.
editorial.synopsis: A star reporter comes into the newsroom to tell her editor and ex-husband that she is quitting to marry an insurance man from Albany and live a normal life. He has other plans. A man is to be hanged in the morning, the reporter is the only one who can write it, and over the next twelve hours in a press room overlooking the gallows the editor lies, schemes, has the fiancé arrested twice, and talks. Hawks had the actors overlap every line and shot the dialogue at nearly twice the speed of normal speech, and Rosalind Russell and Cary Grant made it sound like two people who think faster than anyone else in the room and know it. It is ninety-two minutes and feels like forty.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 129 in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the fastest-talking film ever made; Hawks' gender-swap of The Front Page turned a newspaper farce into the sharpest comedy about work, marriage and the press that Hollywood produced.

editorial.hook: French officers in a German prison camp, and the class that unites their captors.
editorial.synopsis: Two French airmen are shot down in 1916 and taken prisoner — one an aristocrat, one a mechanic turned officer — along with a wealthy Jewish banker's son. The camps are almost civilised: the men stage a revue, dig a tunnel, are moved to a mountain fortress run by a German aristocrat with a neck brace and perfect manners who recognises the French count as the only man there he can really talk to. Renoir, who flew in the war himself, films it with a humane patience that lets every character — German and French, officer and ranker, the farm widow who hides two escapees — have his reasons. It is a war film with almost no war in it, and the most hopeful film ever made about why the hope is misplaced.
editorial.whyItMatters: The first Criterion release, number one on their spine list, and 61st on TSPDT's; banned by Goebbels as 'cinematic public enemy number one', it is the film that made Renoir's humanism a world possession and the model for every prison-camp story that came after.

editorial.hook: Nine lives in the San Fernando Valley over one day, and then the sky does something.
editorial.synopsis: One day in the San Fernando Valley: a dying television producer and his trophy wife, his estranged son who teaches men to seduce women, a game-show host with a secret, a former quiz kid, a current quiz kid, a cop who falls in love with a cocaine addict at the door of her apartment. Anderson, at twenty-nine, weaves them together with an Aimee Mann soundtrack that at one point every character sings along to, in their separate rooms, and then does something at the end that no film had done and that either breaks the film or completes it, depending on how you feel about frogs. It is three hours of enormous emotion, played at full volume, and it believes in coincidence the way other films believe in plot.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Bear at Berlin in 2000 and the film in which Anderson took Altman's Nashville and Short Cuts and pushed them past realism into the operatic; the most sincere and most divisive American film of its decade, and the one that announced its director's refusal to be reasonable.

editorial.hook: A count's daughter, her father's valet, one midsummer night, and the past in the frame.
editorial.synopsis: Midsummer Eve on a Swedish estate. The count is away, the servants are dancing, and his daughter — restless, reckless, half in love with the idea of falling — comes down to the kitchen and begins a game with her father's valet that neither of them can stop. Strindberg's play is one room and one night; Sjöberg opens it, and does something no one had done — lets the characters' memories walk into the same frame as their present, so that the grown Julie sits at a table while her child self and her mother move through the room behind her. It is a film about class and sex and shame, filmed with a formal daring that was years ahead of Bergman, who was Sjöberg's assistant.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1951, shared, and Cahiers' top ten of that year; the film that invented the flashback-in-the-same-shot, a device Resnais and Bergman would make famous, and the proof that Swedish cinema's greatness did not begin with Bergman.

editorial.hook: Three boys at an English public school, a rooftop, a machine gun. Possibly a dream.
editorial.synopsis: A boys' boarding school in England, with its chapel and its canings and its prefects who run the place on behalf of masters who have given up. Three boys in the lower sixth refuse to fit, grow their hair, drink vodka in their study, pin pictures of revolutionaries on the wall. One of them meets a girl in a café and the film becomes, for a scene, a tiger fight on the floor. The film drifts between colour and black and white for reasons Anderson never explained — he said it was budget, and also that it wasn't. The last fifteen minutes, on Founders' Day, are the most famous ending in British cinema and nobody is sure whether they happen. It was released months after Paris, May 1968, and understood as prophecy.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1969 and the central film of the British New Wave's radical wing; Anderson's assault on the institution that produced him, made with a formal freedom — surrealism inside realism — that connects Vigo's Zero for Conduct to the 1960s and gave Malcolm McDowell to Kubrick.

editorial.hook: A twelve-year-old in the rubble of Berlin in 1947, doing what the adults can't.
editorial.synopsis: Berlin, two years after the war, a city of rubble with people living in it. A twelve-year-old boy is the only one in his family who can earn anything: his father is bedridden, his older brother a soldier hiding from registration, his sister trading cigarettes in bars at night. He digs graves, sells scales, steals coal, and falls in with his old schoolteacher, a Nazi still, who tells him the weak must make way for the strong. Rossellini shot the ruins as they were, with a German boy who had never acted, and the film ends in an empty bombed-out building with a child who has done the one thing he thought was asked of him and found out what it means. It is seventy-three minutes and it has no mercy because there was none.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Leopard at Locarno in 1948 and the last and darkest of Rossellini's war trilogy; dedicated to his son who had just died, it is the film in which Neorealism looked at the enemy's children and found the same ruin, and it marked the end of the movement's first phase.

editorial.hook: A boy scout for the Red Army, between dreams of his mother and missions across a swamp.
editorial.synopsis: A twelve-year-old boy, his family killed by the Germans, works as a scout for a Soviet unit on the Eastern Front, crossing the river at night through a flooded forest of dead birch trees to report on enemy positions. The officers want to send him to military school; he refuses, with the fury of someone who has nothing else. Between missions he dreams: his mother at a well, a cart full of apples in the rain, running on a beach with a girl. Tarkovsky's first feature already has his signature — water everywhere, a camera that drifts along surfaces, a dream logic that cuts into the war without warning — and the hard, bright black and white of the swamp scenes is as beautiful as anything he ever filmed.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Lion 1962 for a debut, and the film that made Sartre write an essay in Tarkovsky's defence against Soviet critics who found it too poetic; the first statement of the dream-and-memory method that Mirror would perfect, and the most humane war film made in the Soviet Union before Come and See.

editorial.hook: Two thieves in love, a perfume heiress, and a Venice where the gondolier is the dustman.
editorial.synopsis: A gentleman thief and a pickpocket meet in a Venice hotel, each posing as aristocracy, and fall in love while stealing from each other at dinner — a garter, a watch, a wallet. In Paris they set their sights on a perfume heiress, and the thief takes a job as her secretary, and the problem is that she is lovely and he is not entirely pretending. Lubitsch films it in art-deco rooms with closed doors that tell you everything happening behind them, and the dialogue — Samson Raphaelson's — is a sequence of double meanings so elegant the censors could not find the obscenity they knew was there. It was banned under the Production Code for thirty years. It is the most sophisticated comedy Hollywood ever made.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 136 in the 2022 critics' poll and the film Lubitsch himself called his best; the definition of 'the Lubitsch touch' — sex, money and manners handled so lightly they float — and the model Billy Wilder kept a sign about on his office wall: 'How would Lubitsch do it?'

editorial.hook: A Black optometrist traces her birth mother and finds a white woman who never knew.
editorial.synopsis: A Black optometrist in London, after her adoptive mother's funeral, decides to trace her birth mother, and the records lead to a white woman who works in a cardboard-box factory, lives with her sullen daughter in a terraced house, and has no memory of a Black baby because she never looked. Their first meeting, in a café, is a single unbroken shot of eight minutes in which two women sitting side by side go from denial to the truth to laughter. Leigh built the film through months of improvisation with the actors, and the climax — a barbecue at her brother's house where every secret in the family comes out at once — is as true and as funny and as painful as anything in British cinema.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1996 and the film that took Leigh's method — characters built from months of improvisation, then scripted — to its widest audience; Brenda Blethyn and Marianne Jean-Baptiste's café scene is one of the great two-handers in cinema, and the whole film is a lesson in how to earn a happy ending.

editorial.hook: A Manhattan doctor spends one long night outside his marriage, in a city like a dream.
editorial.synopsis: A wealthy Manhattan doctor and his wife go to a Christmas party and both are tempted; the next night, stoned, she tells him about a naval officer she once saw and would have left him for, and he walks out into the city. The night that follows is a sequence of doors half-opened — a dead patient's daughter, a prostitute, a costume shop with a daughter of its own, a mansion where a masked ritual is in progress and he does not have the password. Kubrick shot New York on a London soundstage and let the streets glow unreally; the Christmas lights are in every frame. It is a film about a marriage, about jealousy as fantasy, and about what a man thinks he wants when he's been told no.
editorial.whyItMatters: Kubrick's last film, Cahiers' film of the year in 1999, and the most misunderstood work in his career — sold as erotica, it is a dream about fidelity in the tradition of Schnitzler and Ophüls, and its reputation has climbed every year since his death.

editorial.hook: A man in an industrial wasteland is given a baby that isn't quite one. The radiator sings.
editorial.synopsis: A man with a shock of upright hair lives in a one-room apartment in an industrial nowhere of pipes, steam and dead ground, and is told by his girlfriend's family that she has had a baby and he must marry her. The baby is a swaddled thing with a lizard's head that cries all night. She leaves. He is alone with it, and with the woman who lives in his radiator and sings about heaven. Lynch made it over five years with a crew of a handful, shooting at night in borrowed stables, and the sound — a constant industrial hum, like living inside a machine — is as much the film as the images. It is a nightmare about fatherhood, about bodies, about dread without an object, and it is also, oddly, tender.
editorial.whyItMatters: Fifty-second in the 2022 Sight & Sound directors' poll and the film that founded the midnight-movie circuit and Lynch's career at once; Kubrick showed it to the crew of The Shining to put them in the right mood, and its sound design changed what a film could do to a body.

editorial.hook: A year in a seaside town under Mussolini, remembered by someone who was a boy there.
editorial.synopsis: A year in Rimini in the 1930s, from the spring puffballs to the next: a boy and his friends, a father who threatens to kill himself at every dinner, a tobacconist with enormous breasts, the village idiot, a blind accordionist, the town beauty everyone calls Gradisca, a Fascist rally, a peacock in the snow, the great ocean liner Rex passing at night with the whole town rowed out in boats to see it. Fellini built the town in the studio and remembered it as a child would — bigger, stranger, funnier — and the episodes have no plot except the seasons. The title is Romagnolo dialect for 'I remember'. It is his warmest film and, underneath the warmth, a portrait of how a people gets taken in.
editorial.whyItMatters: Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film and 77th on TSPDT's list; the fourth Criterion release and Fellini's fullest act of memory — the model for every film that has tried to recall a childhood town as a carnival, from Cinema Paradiso to Roma.

editorial.hook: A man wants so badly to be normal that he becomes a Fascist assassin.
editorial.synopsis: A professor in Mussolini's Italy wants, above everything, to be like everyone else — because of something that happened to him as a boy, which he believes made him different — and so he joins the secret police and volunteers to kill his old mentor, an anti-Fascist exile in Paris. He marries a woman he finds pleasantly stupid and takes her to Paris on honeymoon as cover. Bertolucci and his cinematographer Vittorio Storaro filmed the 1930s as a sequence of enormous rooms, leaf-shadows, Venetian blinds and tilted frames — the asylum, the ministry, a dance hall where two women tango — and made Fascism look exactly as seductive as it was. The assassination in a snowy forest is one of the great sequences in cinema.
editorial.whyItMatters: Eighty-seventh on TSPDT's list and the film Coppola and Storaro's generation learned colour and composition from — the look of The Godfather and Apocalypse Now begins here; a political film that locates Fascism in a man's shame, and the high point of Italian cinema's second golden age.

editorial.hook: A woman in a Calvinist village believes God wants her to save her husband through other men
editorial.synopsis: A simple, devout young woman in a Calvinist village on the Scottish coast marries an oil-rig worker, and the happiness of it frightens her church, which does not allow bells. He is paralysed in an accident on the rig, and from his bed asks her to take lovers and tell him about it — to keep him alive, he says. She believes him. Then she believes God has asked her too. Von Trier shot it hand-held, on grainy film, in chapters introduced by panoramic landscapes under 1970s rock songs, and Emily Watson, in her first film, gives a performance of such openness that the film's cruelty to her is almost impossible to watch. The ending claims a miracle and dares you to refuse it.
editorial.whyItMatters: Grand Prix at Cannes 1996 and the film that made von Trier a world figure; the first of his 'Golden Heart' trilogy and the template for his cinema of female sacrifice — Dancer in the Dark, Dogville — which has been called both the most compassionate and the most sadistic in modern film.

editorial.hook: A Roman prostitute who keeps being robbed of everything, and the smile at the end.
editorial.synopsis: A small, stubborn prostitute on the outskirts of Rome is pushed into the Tiber by a lover who runs off with her handbag in the first scene, and the film is her picking herself up — from that, from a night in a movie star's mansion where she is hidden in the bathroom when his girlfriend returns, from a pilgrimage to a shrine where the miracle does not arrive, from a hypnotist's stage where she confesses in front of a laughing crowd that she wants a home and a husband. Giulietta Masina plays her with a clown's face and a will that nothing can quite break. The last scene — a road, a group of young people with guitars, a face turning toward the camera through tears — is the most hopeful ending ever earned.
editorial.whyItMatters: Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, Best Actress at Cannes 1957 for Masina, and Cahiers' top three of the year; remade as Sweet Charity, and the film in which Fellini's humanism and his wife's genius for pathos are inseparable.

editorial.hook: Twenty-two people in Los Angeles over a few days, and an earthquake at the end.
editorial.synopsis: Nine Raymond Carver stories and a poem, moved from the Pacific Northwest to Los Angeles and braided: a pool cleaner's wife who does phone sex while changing a nappy, a doctor whose son is hit by a car, a baker who leaves threatening messages about an uncollected cake, three fishermen who find a dead woman in the river and keep fishing, a jazz singer and her cellist daughter, a cop who lies to everyone. Altman lets them brush past each other without noticing, cuts freely between twenty-two lives, and lets a medfly spraying campaign and a small earthquake bracket it all. Three hours pass without a plot and with more life than most decades of cinema. Everyone is a little cruel and no one is a villain.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Lion 1993 — shared with Three Colors: Blue — and the film that reconnected Altman to his Nashville method after a decade in the wilderness; the direct model for Magnolia, Crash and the whole ensemble-mosaic genre, and the best screen version of Carver's shrug.

editorial.hook: A Tehran divorce sets off a chain of small lies, and nobody is wrong, and someone is.
editorial.synopsis: A middle-class couple in Tehran sit before a judge: she wants to leave Iran with their eleven-year-old daughter, he will not abandon his father, who has Alzheimer's. The judge refuses the divorce; she moves out; he hires a devout working-class woman to care for the old man, and something happens in the flat one afternoon — a fall, a push, a miscarriage, a lie about where the money went — that drags both families into court and into each other. Farhadi constructs it like a thriller in which the mystery is who is telling the truth, and every answer costs someone. The daughter watches all of it, and the film's last shot is her being asked to choose.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Bear at Berlin in 2011 and the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film — the first for Iran; the film that made Farhadi's moral-puzzle method famous, and the clearest portrait in contemporary cinema of how class, faith and law bear down on one ordinary decision.

editorial.hook: A traveller drifts into a vampire story that unfolds like a half-remembered dream.
editorial.synopsis: A young man obsessed with the occult arrives at a riverside inn and is given a package by an old man who enters his room at night: to be opened on my death. The next day he follows a shadow that walks without a body to a château where a girl is sickening and a doctor is lying, and the film stops being a story and becomes a sequence of visions — shadows dancing on a wall without dancers, a man watching his own burial through a window in the coffin lid, a mill filling with flour. Dreyer shot it through gauze, in a milky light that makes everything look seen through fever, with a cast of amateurs and barely any dialogue. It is the quietest horror film ever made and one of the most frightening.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 146 in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the strangest film of Dreyer's career — a flop that ended his career for a decade; its coffin's-eye view and floating shadows are the ancestor of every dream-logic horror from Lynch to Jonathan Glazer.
